title: Cyrus and the Blue Hour
premise: Emrys Fairweather, once a celebrated piano prodigy who abandoned the stage at nineteen, returns to the Alder Conservatory not as a teacher but as a night janitor, cataloguing silences as carefully as she once catalogued sonatas. When the auction of her late mentor's childhood home surfaces a box of photographs and letters she never knew existed, Emrys discovers that the woman who shaped her life was also a stranger hiding a daughter given up decades ago. As the blue hour before demolition ticks down, Emrys must track down this half-sister, confront her own unfinished grief, and decide whether forgiveness is something you earn or something you give. The novel ends with Emrys playing again — not for an audience, but in the empty house's last hour, while her found family listens from the doorway.
about_author: Ada Crane is the pen name of a former conservatory librarian who spent fifteen years shelving other people's music before writing her own stories. She lives near a tidal estuary and writes exclusively during the hour after sunset.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Emrys, POV, mops the recital hall after midnight and mentally lists everything she has never told anyone: why she stopped playing, whom she left behind. A flyer for an estate auction catches her eye — the address belongs to Marguerite Voss, her childhood mentor. Emotional beat: quiet dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. She attends the preview at the Voss house, moving through rooms that taught her hands their first scales. In a locked display case: photographs of Marguerite with a child who is not Emrys. Emotional beat: the past stops being safe.

chapters.title: Lot 47
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. At the auction she impulsively bids on Lot 47 — a shoebox of letters — and wins it against a sharp-eyed stranger named Dev Anand, an archivist. Emotional beat: first reckless act in twenty years; adrenaline and guilt.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Kept
chapters.summary: Emrys POV, reading letters by lamplight. She learns of 'Talia,' born 1971, surrendered for adoption. The realization lands: she has a sister Marguerite never mentioned. Emotional beat: vertigo — inheritance revealed as concealment.

chapters.title: Dev
chapters.summary: Dev Anand POV. He researches the Voss estate professionally and notices Lot 47 was mislabeled — its contents belong to someone else entirely. He tracks Emrys down, torn between duty and curiosity. Emotional beat: two lonely people circling the same secret.

chapters.title: The Conservatory at Night
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Dev visits the conservatory; they walk the corridors where Emrys once performed. She deflects questions about her career with practiced ease, but he recognizes the name Fairweather from old programs. Emotional beat: guarded connection forming over shared reverence for lost things.

chapters.title: Talia Reyes
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. With Dev's archival skills they locate Talia Reyes, a hospice nurse in coastal Oregon. Emrys writes seven drafts of a letter and sends none. Emotional beat: hope curdling into fear of rejection.

chapters.title: Hands That Remember
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Cleaning the practice rooms, she finds a piano out of tune and, alone, plays four bars before stopping herself, shaking. Dev witnesses it from the doorway without comment. Emotional beat: the body remembers what the mind forbids.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Silence
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Emrys POV, 1998. Marguerite deflects a question about her family with unusual coldness; teenage Emrys learns which doors stay shut. Emotional beat: understanding how silence was inherited like a heirloom.

chapters.title: Oregon
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. She drives to Oregon unannounced and watches Talia from across a parking lot, unable to approach. Talia, sensing being watched, looks directly at her — recognition neither can name yet. Emotional beat: courage failing at the threshold.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Old Photographs
chapters.summary: Talia POV. Talia examines the photograph Emrys finally leaves on her porch: Marguerite holding an infant. Her adoptive mother's deathbed words about 'a woman who chose music over me' resurface. Emotional beat: anger arriving before grief.

chapters.title: Confrontation at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Emrys and Talia POV alternating. On the beach, Talia demands to know why Emrys came. Emrys admits she doesn't know — to apologize for Marguerite, or to claim kinship. Talia walks away. Emotional beat: honesty offered too bluntly breaks instead of bonds.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Back home, she learns the Voss house will be demolished in three weeks unless a preservation bid succeeds. Dev proposes they archive the house properly — and needs Emrys's memories to do it. Emotional beat: deadline transforms mourning into purpose.

chapters.title: Room by Room
chapters.summary: Emrys and Dev POV alternating. Documenting the house together, Emrys narrates memories room by room; Dev records them. In the attic they find Marguerite's own unsent letter to Talia, dated two years before her death. Emotional beat: intimacy deepening through shared excavation.

chapters.title: The Unsent Letter
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Marguerite's letter reveals her shame, her fear Talia would despise her, and a request: that whoever found it play the Chopin Berceuse in the house once. Emrys realizes the request was meant for her all along. Emotional beat: the weight of being trusted with someone's cowardice.

chapters.title: Rift
chapters.summary: Dev POV. Dev submits his archival report and discovers the conservatory board plans to use the house's demolition to fund a new wing bearing Marguerite's name — sanitized, rewritten. He warns Emrys; she accuses him of using her story for his career. Emotional beat: trust fracturing under pressure.

chapters.title: What Forgiveness Is Not
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Alone, Emrys rereads her own inventory of unsaid things and sees how much of it is blame — of Marguerite, of herself. She drafts a letter to Talia that says only true things, no pleas. Emotional beat: humility as turning point.

chapters.title: The Preservation Hearing
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV shifts. At the public hearing, Emrys speaks publicly about Marguerite — flaws, abandonment, love included — derailing the sanitized memorial plan. Dev backs her with the full archive. The board relents: the house will stand, but only if inhabited. Emotional beat: truth as the only effective argument.

chapters.title: A Reply, Postmarked Oregon
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Talia's reply arrives: not absolution, but a question — 'Did she ever play for anyone without an audience?' Emrys understands what is being asked of her. Emotional beat: terror and invitation braided together.

chapters.title: Berceuse
chapters.summary: Emrys POV, climax. On the eve of the house's reopening as a community music school, Emrys sits at Marguerite's piano during the blue hour and plays the Berceuse through, hands trembling, no audience required. Talia stands unseen in the doorway, then steps inside. Emotional beat: performance transformed into offering; the prodigy returns on her own terms.

chapters.title: Two Names on the Deed
chapters.summary: Alternating Emrys and Talia POV. Weeks later: the house is a small teaching studio; Talia has taken leave from hospice work to help run it. They are not close yet, but they are present — sisters learning each other's rhythms like a difficult duet. Emotional beat: found family built slowly, without guarantees.

chapters.title: Coda: Everything Said
chapters.summary: Emrys POV, final chapter. At the conservatory, Emrys resigns her janitorial post and accepts a position teaching adult beginners — people with no prodigy past to live up to. Her new inventory lists things said aloud: apologies, invitations, her own name spoken without flinching. Emotional beat: resolution as beginning; identity reclaimed, quietly.
